Top Stock Market Highlights of the Week: Singapore Banks, NASDAQ Sell-off, Grab and SGX RegCo
article:
This week’s highlights cover bank earnings, a Wall Street sell-off, an upgraded outlook and a regulatory shift for local listings.
Singapore’s three
local banks
reported mixed third-quarter results.
In the US, the NASDAQ suffered its worst day in 19 months on fears of tighter AI regulation.
A leading super-app beat expectations for the quarter and raised its full-year targets.
Closer to home, the bourse’s regulatory arm will take over prospectus reviews from the central bank, a move meant to make listing in Singapore faster and more predictable.
Local banks post mixed third-quarter results
Singapore’s three local banks delivered mixed results for the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026) amid narrowing margins and volatile markets.
DBS Group
(SGX: D05) reported a 5% year-on-year (YoY) fall in net profit to S$2.81 billion, missing the S$2.95 billion consensus forecast as markets trading income plunged 65% to S$152 million.
Even so, the bank raised its quarterly
dividend
to S$0.81 per share, from S$0.75 a year ago.
DBS is also exploring a prime brokerage business, and chairman Peter Seah will hand over to Anthony Lim on 1 January 2027.
OCBC
(SGX: O39) was the only one of the three to beat expectations, with net profit rising 3% to S$2.04 billion.
Its net interest margin (NIM) fell 18 basis points to 1.66%, and lower contributions from insurance arm
Great Eastern Holdings
(SGX: G07) cut non-interest income by 10%.
OCBC nonetheless raised its 2026 loan growth guidance to the low double digits.
UOB
(SGX: U11) posted a 182.2% jump in net profit to S$1.25 billion, but this came off a low base and still missed the S$1.38 billion forecast.
The bank now expects full-year NIM to come in below its earlier guidance of 1.75% to 1.8%, and its shares fell 5% on the day.
NASDAQ slides into correction on AI regulation fears
The NASDAQ Composite fell 5.52% to 24,315.00 on 5 November 2026.
It was the index’s steepest one-day decline since the “Liberation Day” tariff announcement in April 2025.
The drop left the NASDAQ more than 10% below its record close on 6 October 2026, confirming a technical correction.
The S&P 500 fell 4.36% to 7,353.73, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 3.44%.
The sell-off came after the Democrats won control of the US Congress in the midterm elections.
Some of the newly elected officials have opposed new data centres, raising concerns that tighter regulation could slow the AI infrastructure build-out that has driven markets this year.
Chipmakers led the decline, with
NVIDIA Corp
(NASDAQ: NVDA) among the hardest hit.
Qualcomm Inc
(NASDAQ: QCOM) also fell after its smartphone chip sales missed estimates.
Despite the rout, the S&P 500 and NASDAQ remain up 7.4% and 4.6% year to date respectively.
Attention now turns to US jobs data, with traders expecting the Federal Reserve to raise rates again in December.
Grab lifts full-year guidance after an earnings beat
Grab Holdings (NASDAQ: GRAB)
raised its 2026 forecasts on 3 November 2026 after its quarterly results beat expectations.
For 3Q2026, revenue rose 27% YoY to US$1.1 billion, roughly in line with estimates.
Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) jumped 74% to US$237 million, well above the US$194.2 million analysts had projected.
The major technology player added about three million monthly transacting users in the quarter, taking its total to 57 million.
Grab now expects full-year revenue of up to US$4.2 billion and adjusted EBITDA of up to US$800 million.
In August, it had guided for up to US$4.15 billion and US$740 million respectively.
Headwinds remain, as Indonesia has capped commissions on motorcycle ride-hailing and rising fuel prices continue to drive up operating costs.
Additionally, Taiwan’s competition regulator recently blocked Grab’s proposed US$600 million acquisition of Foodpanda’s local business.
Singapore streamlines its IPO approval process
From 4 January 2027, Singapore Exchange Regulation (SGX RegCo), the regulatory subsidiary of
Singapore Exchange Limited
(SGX: S68), will take over the prospectus review functions of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).
This will cover listing applications for both the Mainboard and the Global Listing Board.
Today, issuers file their prospectus with MAS and their listing application with SGX RegCo separately.
Under the new arrangement, both will go to SGX RegCo through a single electronic portal.
Complete applications are expected to be processed within six to eight weeks.
SGX RegCo will also stand down its Listings Advisory Committee to reduce the number of regulatory touchpoints.
SGX RegCo CEO Tan Boon Gin said the change would
streamline initial public offerings
(IPOs) and give issuers more regulatory certainty.
MAS will continue to oversee SGX RegCo and will keep the power to grant prospectus exemptions.
The Equities Market Review Group first proposed the change, which marks a shift towards a disclosure-based regime, where investors, rather than regulators, judge the merits of a listing.

title: Schroders said to seek mall sale in bid to offload Singapore properties
article:
(Nov 7): Schroders plc is planning to sell off some of its real estate assets in Singapore, having appointed a pair of brokers to raise around $220 million from the sale of a mall, according to people familiar with the matter.

The London-based asset manager, which was acquired by Nuveen last month, wants to sell Wisteria Mall, a suburban two-story retail asset in northern Singapore, according to people familiar with the matter. Brokers Knight Frank and Savills plc are running an expression of interest exercise that is due to close in late November, the people said, asking for anonymity to speak about a private process.

The mall was bought in 2022 for $208 million by Schroders’ Pamfleet Real Estate Fund III, according to a media report at the time. It has an occupancy level of 93%, according to the people.

The attempted sale will add to an earlier push to sell off a hotel in the city state that Schroders co-owns with TPG Angelo Gordon. A sale process was conducted by Jones Lang LaSalle Inc for $320 million in 2024, although the asset has yet to be sold.

“We regularly review our real estate portfolios and consider opportunities in the best interests of our investors,” said a spokesperson for Schroders Capital, the firm’s private markets investment arm. A Savills spokesperson declined to comment. A Knight Frank spokesperson didn’t immediately respond to a request for comments.

Commercial property sales in Singapore have soared this year, totalling about US$20 billion ($25.7 billion) in the first three quarters, more than triple from a year earlier, according to MSCI Inc. The boom has been driven in part by softer pricing expectations as owners look to sell off assets, especially as funds begin to mature.

See also: Besides healthcare top pick, Nuveen Real Estate touts grocery-anchored retail in many markets

title: OpenAI completes US$11 bil portion of funding at US$1.25 tril value
article:
(Nov 7): OpenAI has closed on new funding of roughly US$11 billion ($14 billion), the initial part of a round that values the company at US$1.25 trillion, according to people familiar with the matter.

The funding was wired to the company as of Friday, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity as the information is not public. The remainder of the round, which could increase to as much as US$20 billion in total, is expected to be completed in the coming weeks, one person said.

The AI developer has been in talks for more than a month to raise a large funding round after delaying its plans for an initial public offering (IPO). OpenAI initially set out to raise US$30 billion or more at a US$1.4 trillion valuation, Bloomberg News has reported, before scaling back its plans amid a public market rout for the AI sector.

OpenAI declined to comment. The Wall Street Journal previously reported some details of the funding.

Investors that contributed to the first funding close include Coatue Management and T Rowe Price, the people said. Other investors in the round include SoftBank Group Corp, Sequoia Capital, Founders Fund and Andreessen Horowitz, people said. A syndicate of backers from the United Arab Emirates also joined, Bloomberg News has reported.

OpenAI is also working with investment banks to raise from high-net-worth individuals and retail investors, the people said.

See also: Nvidia boosts chip tracking in Southeast Asia to fight smuggling — Bloomberg

Softbank, Founders Fund and T Rowe Price declined to comment. Coatue, Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia didn't immediately respond to requests for comments.

The reduced funding goals represent a stark shift for a fundraising juggernaut that helped usher in the current artificial intelligence (AI) boom. The sentiment around AI has also changed dramatically since the round kicked off, due to concerns about the spending spree on physical infrastructure for AI and the potential for new roadblocks to data centre construction following the US midterm elections.

Prospective investors in OpenAI rival Anthropic PBC’s upcoming IPO are also rethinking the Claude maker’s valuation. Potential buyers are discussing about a US$1.2 trillion to US$1.3 trillion valuation range for Anthropic, Bloomberg News has reported, down from US$1.5 trillion previously.

See also: AI elite lose US$18 bil as chip stock rout spreads to Asia

OpenAI most recently raised US$122 billion in a March funding round at an US$852 billion valuation.

title: US believes woman close to Nvidia CEO a China spy — report
article:
(Nov 7): US intelligence officials told the Trump administration that a woman who had become close to Nvidia Corp chief executive officer Jensen Huang was working for a Chinese spy agency, which recruited her to collect information on him, The New York Times reported on Friday.

The newspaper cited unnamed sources who it said had been told of American surveillance conducted on the woman, Alice Huang, an executive with an Asian technology company called Megaspeed International. Administration officials learned of the accusations in an intelligence memo, the Times said.

Alice Huang was working for Beijing’s Ministry of State Security, which was manoeuvring to glean more detail about American artificial intelligence (AI) chips, according to the Times, and possibly persuade Nvidia to try to make its most sophisticated semiconductors available to the Chinese.

It was not clear when or how she met Jensen Huang.

The Financial Times (FT), in an article published on Friday night, said US officials believe that the relationship was romantic.

The case has taken on new urgency following this week’s US midterm elections, which will give Democrats control of Congress. Republicans also are scrutinising Jensen Huang’s ties to the alleged spy.

See also: EU escalates TikTok probe over algorithmic ‘rabbit holes’

The House Select Committee on China said in a statement on Thursday that it had sent a letter to Jensen Huang “requesting his participation in a joint, closed-door briefing”.

“The letter details the lawmakers’ concerns regarding [Jensen] Huang’s interactions with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, a publicly reported Chinese intelligence asset, and the company’s security protocols against foreign adversary espionage,” the panel said in the statement.

Megaspeed is part of Nvidia’s cloud partner (NCP) network. The Singapore-based company buys equipment from the chipmaker and rents out computing power to AI developers.

Nvidia said in a statement after the Times article was published that its cloud partners “do not ask us to seek changes in US law or advocate for sales to China”. The company added that “anyone seeking classified information through our NCP customers would have hit a dead end. We neither have nor share classified information with customers”.

Asked about the FT report regarding a possible romantic relationship, Nvidia referred to previous comments by Jensen Huang that he had a typical business relationship with Alice Huang.

The Central Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence did not immediately respond to requests for comments on Friday evening.

In an interview last week, Jensen Huang defended his dealings with Megaspeed, calling them “normal and not unusual”, while stressing that the company has checked to ensure that Megaspeed didn’t illegally send Nvidia’s AI processors to China.

title: With Jim Rogers on board, Catalist-board SDAI eyes anti-ageing market for eventual trading resumption
article:
With famed billionaire investor Jim Rogers on its board of directors, SDAI Limited is embarking on transforming its business, with a new focus on longevity and healthy ageing.

Previously known as Kitchen Culture Holdings, the company was a distributor of kitchen and home furnishings. The counter has been under a trading suspension since July 2021 and was rebranded into SDAI in November 2023.

Rogers holds an 8.55% interest in OOWAY Group, a controlling shareholder of the SDAI. He was appointed non-executive and non-independent board director in June 2023.

Diversifying into biotechnology, SDAI aims to bridge “cutting-edge” longevity science, “innovative” technologies and everyday wellbeing, by introducing science-backed anti-ageing, longevity and biological age management solutions to Asian markets.

Asia-Pacific’s anti-ageing market is expected to reach US$20.6 ($26.4) billion in 2025 and is forecast to grow at a compounded annual growth rate of 8% to reach US$38.1 billion by 2033. According to the Asian Development Bank, Apac is rapidly ageing, with one in four people in the region to reach over 60 years old by 2050. The population of older persons (aged over 60) in the region will triple between 2010 and 2050, reaching close to 1.3 billion people.

Presumably to serve this growing market, the company launched, on Nov 6, its SDAI BioAge Core product, a dietary supplement, researched and developed by longevity scientist Brian Kennedy, Distinguished Professor of Biochemistry and Physiology at the National University Singapore’s (NUS) Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine.

See also: Silver opportunity: Armed with ‘gerontechnology’, LHN debuts Jubiliv with five units at Boon Lay

The product will be progressively rolled-out in China, Hong Kong and Macau, subject to regulatory approval.

Attending the product launch, 84 year-old Rogers says that he is keen to try the supplement. “Of course I will. Why not? I want to live forever,” he quips with a smile.

Separately, the firm announced on Nov 4 that it had established a scientific board to guide itsscientific strategy and support its transformation into a longevity-focused biotechnology company. This scientific board is chaired by Kennedy and includes four other researchers in the field.

See also: Is silver talent the silver bullet? Why Asia's ageing workforce is the key to solving talent shortages

Chaired by Kennedy, other members of the scientific board are Liou Yih-Cherng, associate professor in NUS’s biological sciences department; Li Rong, a platform expert in metabolomics and lipidomics at Fudan University’s Institute of Metabolism and Integrative Biology; Victor Yu, principal investigator at Tianjian Laboratory of Advanced Biomedical Sciences, Zhengzhou University; and He Chong, principal investigator at the Asian Academy of Anti-Aging and Translational Medicine.

While the transformation remains at an early stage, the company believes that strengthening its scientific capabilities will support differentiated offerings, new revenue opportunities and sustainable long-term value for shareholders.

SDAI CEO Liu Ting told The Edge Singapore that the company is aiming to build up the new business segment first before exploring the resumption of trading of its shares on the stock exchange.

On July 16, executive chairperson and deemed controlling shareholder Hao Dongting extended an interest-free $200,000 loan to the company to support working capital and settle current liabilities.The loan matures at end-2027.

Under the terms of the loan, SDAI has the option to convert the loan into new shares, which would be subscribed by Hao. The subscription price for these new shares will be at a 10% discount to the weighted average price of SDAI shares traded on the relevant market day, subject to the terms of the subscription agreement and the necessary approvals.

SDAI was suspended after calling a trading halt due to suspected payroll irregularities and internal control lapses in 2021. A boardroom tussle subsequently ensued, ending with five directors resigning and five new ones elected, with Rogers one the new five.

For 1HFY2026 ended June 30, SDAI reported a net loss of around $1.73 million, on revenue of $0.25 million.

title: Wall Street grapples with US$5.7 tril rout as AI bets unwind
article:
(Nov 7): Months of unease over Wall Street’s artificial-intelligence (AI) boom erupted into a global market convulsion this week, opening a dangerous new chapter for the investment frenzy that has helped power stock prices, corporate spending and economic growth.

The worries have been on display all year: stretched valuations, mounting debt and doubts about the payoff from trillions of dollars in AI spending. But the Democratic sweep of Congress has added a new political threat, raising the prospect of restrictions on the vast data-center buildout underpinning the boom.

The response has been extraordinary even by the standards of a volatile year. Wednesday brought a sharp – and unexpected — rally in US stocks. Thursday saw a US$2.3 trillion ($3.0 trillion) wipeout in the Nasdaq 100. At the close, 57% of its constituents had fallen at least 20% from their highs, a greater proportion than when the index itself entered a bear market in March 2022. By Friday, chipmakers had rebounded even as strong jobs data reinforced bets on another US Federal Reserve (Fed) interest-rate increase.

The reversals offer a glimpse of how disorderly the next phase of the AI cycle could become — with little help from the usual rescuers. The Fed remains focused on inflation, with traders betting on another interest-rate increase in December. Weakened by the midterm election, US President Donald Trump faces new constraints on fiscal support and may have less incentive to shore up a stock market whose recent losses he has already blamed on the Democrats.

“There are going to be losers, and not everybody who’s investing all of this money in capex is going to be a winner,” said Joe Gubler, a portfolio manager at Causeway Capital Management, which oversees about US$76 billion.

See also: Monster shares fall as weaker margins highlight cost burden

Even retail traders, normally eager to buy market dips, joined the selling at a pace rarely seen since the pandemic. Wall Street’s investment machinery made matters worse. Hedge funds, leveraged investors and automated strategies added to the pressure, making it harder to tell how much of the rout reflected genuine doubts about AI and how much was driven by forced selling.

By Thursday’s close, the US stock market had lost US$5.7 trillion in value since its Oct 6 peak, according to an index tracking total equity market capitalisation.

Finding new market leaders is another challenge. Investors had begun rotating towards cheaper, less glamorous sectors like utilities and consumer staples well before the election. But Thursday’s rout exposed the limits of that escape, with the new favourites failing to withstand the collapse in Big Tech.

See also: US tech stocks rebound as investors weigh valuations after rout

There is a powerful counterweight: Oil prices have plunged on hopes that the Iran war will wind down. That offers relief from inflationary pressures that have squeezed consumers and businesses throughout Trump’s tariff-heavy presidency, though those benefits would take time to emerge.

The rotation was already gathering force before the election. Growth stocks trailed value shares by 10 percentage points in October, their biggest monthly gap since 2001, just a month after their strongest showing in more than a year.

The whiplash is a cross-asset story. Equities swung from outperforming Treasuries by five percentage points to their worst relative showing since early 2025 over the last two months. A popular momentum strategy also surrendered almost all its September gains in October.

Andrew Lapthorne, Societe Generale’s head of quantitative research, traces much of the turmoil to crowded positions built around AI and oil. As those trades reversed, investors were forced to sell technology shares they had favoured and buy back defensive stocks they had bet against, driving even sharper swings.

“You’ve got a mixed combination of people being heavily positioned in one set of assets, and then having to rapidly cover if you’re long-short,” he said. “It could be people with risk budgets where it only takes a few things to then start having some kind of margin call unwind.”

Morgan Stanley data show hedge funds have reduced gross leverage from its June peak by the most in more than a decade. Its quantitative strategists reckon the liquidation may be nearing exhaustion, though they anticipate another market low following a brief rebound.

Lapthorne sees little evidence that the selling reflects a sudden turn towards economic pessimism. And not every investor has been caught out.

Jeff Muhlenkamp exited almost all his fund’s AI holdings before the rout. His US$275 million portfolio was roughly flat for November and ahead of the S&P 500 for the year.

“We sold what was expensive and popular, and bought what was cheap and forgotten,” he said. “When momentum changes, we benefit.”

The economy may be holding up, and the forced selling may soon end. But investors want proof their AI investments will pay off — just as the shift in Washington throws up obstacles to building the infrastructure needed to make them work.

“The aggressive speed of the AI spend, you have to assume that will be at a more deliberate pace,” said Rick Rieder, the chief investment officer of global fixed income at BlackRock Inc on Bloomberg Television. “That changed this week and you have to factor that into your calculus.”

title: China Sunsine issues profit guidance for 3QFY2026, expects ‘significant improvement’ in revenue and profit after tax
article:
China Sunsine says that it is expected to see a “significant improvement” in its revenue and profit after for 3QFY2026 ended Sept 30, as compared to the corresponding quarter.

China Sunsine explains that the expected revenue and profit growth was mainly driven by increase in both the average selling price and sales volume of its core products.

China Sunsine will be releasing its 3QFY2026 business update on Nov 13.

Shares in China Sunsine closed 0.5 cents higher, or up 0.85% at 59 cents on Nov 6.

title: TSMC said to mull making advanced AI memory chips
article:
(Nov 7): Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) is considering broadening its business to include advanced memory chip manufacturing, The Information reported, a move that would give the world’s largest chipmaker an even bigger share of the artificial intelligence (AI) hardware supply chain.

The Taiwanese company recently began drafting plans to produce a particular type of advanced memory chips, known as 3D DRAM, at the request of Nvidia Corp, its biggest customer, The Information reported, citing two people familiar with the plans.

TSMC said in a statement that the company is focused “on our core business at all times”, adding that it’s dedicated to manufacturing chips designed by other companies. While TSMC didn’t address memory chips specifically, the firm said its mission is to be “the trusted technology and capacity provider” of logic chips, which process data as opposed to storing it.

Memory chips have been in severe shortage due to a boom in demand for AI hardware, sending prices soaring and prompting chip designers like Nvidia and Apple Inc to seek additional sourcing. Apple raised the prices for some of its products earlier this year, citing rising memory costs.

title: Anthropic IPO buyers see valuation as low as US$1.1 tril
article:
(Nov 7): Anthropic PBC’s initial public offering (IPO) plans ran into a punishing post-election selloff, prompting a rethink among prospective investors of the company’s expected valuation.

Ahead of the artificial intelligence (AI) lab kicking off formal IPO marketing next week, potential buyers are discussing about a US$1.2 trillion to US$1.3 trillion valuation range for the company, according to people familiar with the matter. Some are weighing a value as low as US$1.1 trillion, one of the people said.

Investors considering bids previously told bankers on the IPO that their estimate of a fair valuation had moved to around US$1.4 trillion to US$1.5 trillion, Bloomberg News has reported. That has shifted again after the Nasdaq 100 index plunged 6.4% on Thursday, wiping out US$2.3 trillion in market value, a record for a single day.

Deliberations are ongoing and no final decisions have been made, said the people, who asked not to be identified as the information isn’t public. A spokesperson for Anthropic declined to comment.

A volatile environment for tech stocks has already dented the outlook for what would be the first IPO by a so-called frontier AI model maker. Investors estimated a fair valuation for Anthropic as high as US$2 trillion in early October, people familiar with the matter have said. The retreat to around US$1.4 trillion to US$1.5 trillion came after a company briefing on its latest financials in October, Bloomberg News reported at the time.

See also: Dubai firm raises US$529 mil in UAE’s first IPO of the year

Questions about the Claude chatbot maker’s valuation in the IPO accelerated after the Democratic sweep of Congress triggered the prospect of greater scrutiny over the pace and impact of data centre expansion. The Cboe Volatility Index rose to the highest since April 2025 on Thursday, making any IPO more difficult for investors to stomach.

One potential limiting factor for Anthropic is the battle to stay ahead of rival OpenAI’s valuation. Anthropic leapfrogged OpenAI in May, raising money privately at a US$965 billion value. OpenAI is targeting a US$1.25 trillion pre-money valuation in its latest funding round, Bloomberg News reported.

Max Kettner, chief multi-asset strategist at HSBC Holdings plc, said around US$1 trillion could be a more comfortable level for the valuation, reducing the risk of elevated volatility once trading begins.

See also: Temasek’s Mapletree said to pick banks for Singapore IPO

“I don’t think we need the headline ‘oh my god, it is a trillion dollar IPO,’ because I think what’s actually more important is the secondary,” Kettner told Bloomberg Radio. “If we get a dynamic like we had with SpaceX, that you get it on secondary and then stock rips for a couple hours, but then it dumps, in the current environment you don’t want to have that.”

Anthropic and its selling shareholders may start the formal marketing with a conservative size and valuation target and increase it based on a positive initial response from investors. Chipmaker Cerebras Systems Inc and design software firm Figma Inc raised more than they indicated in their initial marketing as bankers gauged rising demand. However, both are now trading well below their IPO prices.

Another, less palatable option is for Anthropic to delay its plans. Companies have to have their IPO filings available to the public for at least 15 calendar days before they can begin formal marketing, typically followed by pricing and trading a week later, but some choose to wait weeks or even months after filing publicly to kick off marketing, updating additional quarterly financial data to keep their disclosures fresh.

Michael Field, chief equity strategist at Morningstar, thinks Anthropic would accept a lower valuation if that’s what the market gives them.

“The cost both physically and reputationally of delaying the IPO that might hurt the valuation more in the longer term, whereas if markets hold up at the level that they are, they’ll just get it done at a slightly lower valuation, suck it up and move on,” Field said.

title: Monster shares fall as weaker margins highlight cost burden
article:
(Nov 7): Monster Beverage Corp shares fell as much as 8.2% on Friday, the biggest decline in over two years, after the energy drink giant’s weaker-than-expected margins underscored the impact of soaring costs in the beverage industry.

Third-quarter (3Q) gross profit margin was 54.7%, down from 55.7% a year ago and short of the 55.4% analysts had estimated.

Monster and other beverage companies have been grappling with higher costs due to the impact of US tariffs and the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which have driven up the price of the aluminium used for their cans. Monster expects continued increases in aluminium costs through at least the first quarter of 2027, executives said on a call with analysts on Thursday.

Smaller rival Celsius Holdings Inc also warned that stubbornly high commodity costs are weighing on its margins.

Monster’s 3Q sales rose more than expected, as the energy drink giant continues to see booming demand for its beverages outside of the US. But pricing for Monster’s drinks in international markets tends to be substantially lower than in the US, adding further pressure on profitability.

See also: US tech stocks rebound as investors weigh valuations after rout

The company saw continued strength abroad, driven by Brazil, with sales in the international segment jumping 28% to represent nearly half of Monster’s overall sales in the period. Total net sales rose 17% to US$2.56 billion, ahead of the US$2.49 billion analysts were expecting.

While the commodity costs “aren’t helping,” a US price increase planned for November should help offset some of the compression, Jefferies analysts led by Kaumil Gajrawala wrote in a post-earnings note. “The top line matters more, and it’s intact,” they added.

As demand for beverages that aren’t typical sodas or coffees explodes, Monster has been trying to get its products in front of new costumers that are trying energy drinks for the first time. It’s expanding its social media presence, highlighting both longtime offerings and new launches, including a forthcoming protein energy drink.

See also: Nasdaq 100 sinks 6% as chipmaker selloff deepens

It’s also seeing growth in multipacks as consumers look for value, but isn’t being hit as hard by the consumer pullback that’s hammered restaurants and fast food. “Energy drinks always have been regarded as an affordable luxury,” Chief executive officer Hilton Schlosberg said on the call.

title: 莱佛士医疗首席财务官任职一年多后将离职
减持SpaceX、买入英特尔 淡马锡第三季在美市有什么动作？
